hero.title: Explore what is happening above, on and beneath the surface.
hero.subtitle: Explore the changing Baltic Sea through scientific models, historical assessments and environmental data.
hero.body: This public prototype combines marine science, environmental context and an interactive map so more people can understand the sea as a living system rather than a technical dataset.

temperature.title: Surface temperature
temperature.subtitle: How warm or cold is the water near the surface?

sections.heading: What does it show?
sections.body: The colours show the temperature in the model’s top water layer. Sunlight, wind and the seasons all change it.

sections.heading: How do we know?
sections.body: This map uses a computer model, not direct measurements at every point. Temperature can also be measured by satellites, buoys and ships.

sections.heading: Why does it matter?
sections.body: Fish and other sea life need suitable temperatures. Warm water can hold less oxygen. Very warm periods can put animals and plants under stress.

sections.heading: How can the impacts be reduced?
sections.body: Cutting greenhouse-gas emissions limits long-term warming. Cleaner water and healthy coastal habitats help sea life cope with heat.

sections.heading: What changes with the climate?
sections.body: Warming can make hot periods longer. It can also strengthen [stratification](stratification): water forms layers that mix less easily, so less oxygen may reach deeper water.

currents.title: Currents
currents.subtitle: Where does the water move, and how fast?

sections.heading: What does it show?
sections.body: Currents are moving seawater. Colours show its speed; direction views show where it moves. Wind and differences in water level, salt and temperature help drive it.

sections.heading: How do we know?
sections.body: These values come from a computer model. Instruments on buoys, ships and the seabed can measure currents directly.

sections.heading: Why does it matter?
sections.body: Currents carry heat, salt, oxygen and small animals. They also carry pollution from one place to another.

sections.heading: How can the impacts be reduced?
sections.body: Reducing pollution at its source keeps currents from spreading it. Better wastewater treatment and plans for oil spills help protect coasts.

sections.heading: What changes with the climate?
sections.body: Changes in wind, rainfall and water temperature can change how water moves and where heat and pollution collect.

sections.heading: What does it show?
sections.body: Salinity means the amount of salt in water. The Baltic mixes fresh river water with saltier water from the North Sea. It is generally saltier towards the west and less salty towards the north and east.

sections.heading: How do we know?
sections.body: The map shows model estimates. Researchers also use sensors that measure how easily electricity passes through water to work out its salt content.

sections.heading: Why does it matter?
sections.body: Different species need different amounts of salt. Saltier water is heavier and can sit beneath fresher water, making it harder for oxygen to reach the bottom.

sections.heading: How can the impacts be reduced?
sections.body: We cannot easily control the sea’s salt content. Protecting a range of habitats gives sea life more places to live as conditions change.

sections.heading: What changes with the climate?
sections.body: Rainfall and river flow affect how much fresh water enters the Baltic. Changes can alter its salt content and the mixing of water layers.

oxygen.title: Surface dissolved oxygen
oxygen.subtitle: These existing files show surface oxygen, not oxygen at the seabed.

sections.heading: What does it show?
sections.body: Dissolved oxygen is oxygen mixed into water that animals can use to breathe. These files use the model’s top layer; its exact depth was not saved. They cannot show whether bottom water is short of oxygen. Bottom values will be used after the next manual data update.

sections.heading: How do we know?
sections.body: The map uses a computer model. Sensors lowered from ships can measure oxygen at different depths. Each time shown here represents a daily average.

sections.heading: Why does it matter?
sections.body: Fish and many bottom-dwelling animals need oxygen. When there is too little, they may leave the area or die. The colours show oxygen amounts, not a tested safe-or-unsafe classification.

sections.heading: How can the impacts be reduced?
sections.body: Less fertiliser and wastewater reaching the sea means less excess algae. When dead algae break down, they use up oxygen. Wetlands and better wastewater treatment can help.

sections.heading: What changes with the climate?
sections.body: Warmer water holds less oxygen. [Stratification](stratification), when water stays in layers that mix poorly, can also stop fresh oxygen reaching the bottom.

sections.heading: What does it show?
sections.body: Colours show [significant wave height](waves): roughly the average height of the highest third of waves. Individual waves can be much higher. Wind, water depth and the shape of the coast affect the waves.

sections.heading: How do we know?
sections.body: These are wave-model estimates. Buoys and other instruments can also measure waves. This prototype is for exploration, not a navigation or safety forecast.

sections.heading: Why does it matter?
sections.body: Waves move sand, wear away coasts and affect ferries, harbours and work at sea. They also disturb plants and animals in shallow water.

sections.heading: How can the impacts be reduced?
sections.body: Protecting dunes and coastal wetlands can reduce damage. Keeping buildings away from exposed shores also lowers risk.

sections.heading: What changes with the climate?
sections.body: Changes in storms and sea ice can change wave exposure. With less winter ice, some shores are exposed to waves for longer.

seaLevel.title: Sea level
seaLevel.subtitle: How high is the sea surface?

sections.heading: What does it show?
sections.body: Sea level is the height of the water compared with a reference level. Wind and air pressure can raise or lower it. The exact reference level was not saved in this export.

sections.heading: How do we know?
sections.body: This layer is intended for model values when published. Water-level gauges at the coast can measure sea level directly. Missing data are shown as unavailable.

sections.heading: Why does it matter?
sections.body: High water can flood low coasts, especially during storms. These prototype values are not local flood warnings.

sections.heading: How can the impacts be reduced?
sections.body: Leave space for water, protect coastal wetlands and plan drainage and buildings for future water levels.

sections.heading: What changes with the climate?
sections.body: The global sea level is rising. Local change around the Baltic also depends on whether the land is rising, so the risk differs between coasts.

noise.title: Underwater noise
noise.subtitle: Human-made sound can disturb life below the surface.

sections.heading: What does it show?
sections.body: This layer shows earlier assessments of noise and reported loud events, such as driving piles into the seabed. It is not a live microphone feed.

sections.heading: How do we know?
sections.body: The map combines model assessments and activity reports. Underwater microphones can measure sound directly, but that is not what these map colours show.

sections.heading: Why does it matter?
sections.body: Many animals use sound to find food, communicate and move around. Extra noise can hide these sounds or disturb feeding and breeding.

sections.heading: How can the impacts be reduced?
sections.body: Quieter ships, lower speeds in sensitive areas and quieter construction methods can help. Timing noisy work around breeding seasons also matters.

sections.heading: What changes with the climate?
sections.body: Warming does not directly make this human noise. But animals already stressed by heat or oxygen loss may have more difficulty coping with noise too.

infrastructure.title: Coastal and marine infrastructure
infrastructure.subtitle: Where transport, energy and coastal life meet the sea.

sections.heading: What does it show?
sections.body: The layer shows selected ports, shipping routes, cables, pipelines, wind farms and power plants. It also gives a broad picture of how nearby land is used.

sections.heading: How do we know?
sections.body: These are collected reference records. Positions may be approximate and the list is not complete. This layer stays the same when you change the ocean timeline.

sections.heading: Why does it matter?
sections.body: These places support transport and energy, but building and operating them can disturb habitats or add pollution.

sections.heading: How can the impacts be reduced?
sections.body: Careful siting, cleaner ports and protection of sensitive habitats can reduce damage. Plan projects with marine life in mind from the start.

sections.heading: What changes with the climate?
sections.body: Rising water levels and changing coastlines affect buildings and transport. New offshore energy projects also need space and careful planning.

oxygenBottom.title: Bottom dissolved oxygen
oxygenBottom.subtitle: Oxygen in the deepest available water cell at each place in the model.
oxygenBottom.body: This layer takes the deepest non-missing oxygen value at each location. The depth changes from place to place and is shown when you select a cell. It is a model estimate near the bottom, not a direct measurement at the seabed.
